climbing_route.label: SE ridge scree and broken rock
climbing_route.notes: Leave the maintained tread at Foggy Lake's outlet for an intermittent, cairned climber's path onto the SE ridge. Stay in the scree climber's-right of the crest rather than on the crest itself, following cairns past a small tarn at the base of a snowfield and up broken rock to the base of the summit block. In early season snow can bury the cairned line, making route-finding the main hazard.

climbing_route.label: Summit block
climbing_route.notes: Just below the summit block, many parties inadvertently stray climber's-left onto exposed Class 4 rock; the correct line is the easier one to the right of that.

climbing_route.label: Boot path to the north summit
climbing_route.notes: Leave the PCT at the large, distinctive stump partially blocking the left side of the trail at about 5,200 ft — roughly 15 feet beyond it a boot path forks right (east) and climbs straight uphill. Follow it for the final ~400-500 vertical feet to the northernmost (highest) summit: steep, loose dirt and scree with occasional hands-on Class 2 moves. Snow can linger in the boot-path gully well into early summer. No water past the Commonwealth Creek crossings.

climbing_route.label: East ridge crest (alternative, not the standard route)
climbing_route.notes: Parties who overshoot the stump and continue on the PCT to where it crosses the ridge on the east side can scramble the ridge crest south to the true summit. Abundant loose rock, and notably more exposed and dangerous than the boot path — explicitly not the standard route.

climbing_route.label: Climbers' trail up the west side
climbing_route.notes: At the unsigned junction roughly 2.5 mi along the Klahhane Ridge Trail, a distinct unmaintained climbers' trail splits left (west) — the start of the true scramble. The primitive use trail climbs steeply through rocky meadows and thinning forest on the peak's west side: only about 0.6 mi but roughly 800 of the route's 2,100 ft of gain (average grade ~27%, max ~42%), topping out around 6,000 ft at the base of the summit block/gully. Sustained exposure along the open ridge crest below.

climbing_route.label: Traverse to the summit gully
climbing_route.notes: Do not scramble the first notch you reach — stay on the faint boot path traversing higher to the actual summit gully. Rotten, consolidated snow can choke the summit notch/gully well into July and August even in normal years.

climbing_route.label: Final summit block
climbing_route.notes: Most parties scramble the right/east side of the final block on loose, fractured 'rotten' rock — the same line the descent explicitly avoids downclimbing. Brief but exposed final moves to the true summit at 6,454 ft. Loose scree and rockfall-prone rock throughout the upper scramble.

climbing_route.label: South Chute
climbing_route.notes: A long, narrowing scree gully out of Avalanche Canyon. Start angling up it as soon as the twin rock towers called the 'Cat Ears' come into view above — entering here rather than lower gets you onto firmer, less-eroded ground. About 1,900 ft of scree to a saddle/notch near 6,560-6,600 ft below the Cat Ears; snow-covered and easier in June, bare and miserable by late summer.

climbing_route.label: Second gully to the 7,300 ft notch
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle, descend a short ~150 ft, then climb a second scree gully to a ridge notch near 7,300 ft. Loose talus and scree throughout.

climbing_route.label: The upper 'maze' — Terrible or Finger Traverse
climbing_route.notes: Two options from the notch: the Terrible Traverse, an airy snow-and-rock traverse above a huge cliff at roughly 7,435 ft where a fall would be fatal (several snow pickets advisable for protection in early season); or the Finger Traverse, a downsloping, fingers-jammed-in-a-crack ledge above another cliff, marked by old rusty pitons that some parties use as a solo-belay anchor. Both feed into class 3, occasionally class 4 terrain leading to the base of the ~60 ft summit block.

climbing_route.label: North Chimney on the summit block
climbing_route.notes: The ~60 ft summit block is climbed by its north side; graded 3rd class but reported by many as feeling like easy 4th class. Tops out at the 7,756 ft summit.

climbing_route.label: Blue Glacier and Snow Dome
climbing_route.notes: From the moraine crest, glacier travel begins: descend onto and cross the crevassed Blue Glacier roped as a team, then climb the broad snow dome (Snow Dome) that most Olympus parties also ascend. Expect open crevasses requiring standard roped glacier travel.

climbing_route.label: Upper massif traverse to Mount Tom
climbing_route.notes: Rather than continuing toward Olympus's summit, split off Snow Dome and traverse horizontally along the snowy upper massif, staying below the main Olympus peaks, until it connects with Mount Tom's own White Glacier on its NE slope — or drop via the Hubert Glacier on the south side to reach the Mount Tom-Olympus connecting ridge. Open crevasses on the White/Hubert glaciers too; rope up.

climbing_route.label: Summit block scramble
climbing_route.notes: A final class 3-4 scramble over loose rock to the summit block. Water above Glacier Meadows is glacier-melt/snowmelt only.

climbing_route.label: Descent from Tin Can Gap onto the Queest-Alb Glacier
climbing_route.notes: From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier. Early season this is a straightforward snow descent; by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July). Crevasses open by mid-summer, so rope up as a team when the glacier is snow-covered.

climbing_route.label: Glacier crossing and climb to the Middle-North col
climbing_route.notes: Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak, on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock. This climb is the route-finding crux.

climbing_route.label: Ramp and shallow chimney to the North Peak summit
climbing_route.notes: From the col, follow a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney. Sustained 4th-class with a few low-5th-class exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block. A harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but most parties avoid it for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, rope and harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season.
